processing: Not well documented. As the name and category suggest, it is a green tea of tender buds, made without the sealed yellowing step of the county's better-known Huoshan Huangya.
harvest_season: Not well documented; as with other Anhui bud greens, early spring is the expected picking.
appearance_dry: The name, cuiya, means emerald bud; expect green, bud-heavy leaf as with other Anhui bud greens.
appearance_liquor: Typical of Anhui spring greens: pale yellow-green and clear.
appearance_wet: Typical of Anhui bud greens: soft green buds.
taste_profile: No dependable tasting record exists for this tea; expect a fresh, gently sweet Anhui spring green.

brewing.notes: General advice for a tender bud green: cool water and an open vessel.

vintage_note: Details are few; as is usual for Anhui bud greens, expect it to be sold as the current year's spring harvest and drunk within a year.
description:
Huoshan Cuiya is a green tea name from Huoshan county in Anhui, the same county that gives us the far more famous yellow tea Huoshan Huangya. Cuiya means emerald bud, which is about all the name promises.

Little is documented about how it is made. The main thing to keep in mind is the difference from Huangya: yellow tea goes through a sealed yellowing stage, while a green tea should not.

Treat it as you would other Anhui bud greens. Use water around 80 C and short steeps, and expect something fresh and gently sweet rather than the softened, mellow Huangya cup.

When buying, check the Chinese characters, as 翠芽 and 黄芽 are easily confused, and ask for the picking date. If a seller cannot say what makes this lot different from Huangya, take care.
history: Little is documented about this tea: there is no reliable record of its first production, maker or date. Huoshan's tea reputation rests on Huoshan Huangya, and this name should not be read as sharing that history.
